finding.claim: The avatar endpoint fetches a user-supplied URL server-side. The only check is that the string starts with "https://". There is no host, IP or port allowlist, and no private-address blocking. axios follows redirects by default. An attacker can therefore reach internal HTTPS services, for example https://users.internal or https://169.254.169.254, or any host that redirects to an internal target. A redirect to http:// is also followed, so the https-only check is bypassed. The response size is returned to the caller, so this works as a blind and size-oracle SSRF.

trace.note: only checks typeof string and startsWith('https://')
axios.get(url) is called with the unvalidated URL and follows redirects by default (maxRedirects 5)
img.data.length is returned to the attacker

finding.guards_checked: The only guard is a scheme prefix check. It does not stop https://localhost, https://internal-host, https://[::1], https://10.x.x.x or https://169.254.169.254. It does not check the resolved IP, so DNS rebinding also works. It does not restrict redirects, so an attacker-controlled https server can 302 to http://internal. There is no allowlist and no authentication on the route.

verdict.guard_found: none (only typeof string and startsWith("https://") prefix check at server.js:11; no auth middleware, only express.json())
verdict.reason: server.js:10 takes req.body.avatarUrl from an unauthenticated route, server.js:11 only checks the "https://" prefix, and server.js:14 passes it to axios.get (which follows redirects by default), returning the response byte length at server.js:15. Minor nit: the claim says the check is bypassed through a redirect to http://, but the finding is valid regardless.
